title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Deployment Guide, Reference Architectures, Day-2 Ops, Upgrade & Rollback, and Customer Requirements Library
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices, reference architectures, and operational procedures for private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It is intended for platform engineers, integration engineers, and customer success engineers responsible for designing, deploying, and operating Private (VPC / on-prem) installations of the Redwood inference platform. The guide covers: reference architectures, VPC deployment patterns, on-prem packaging and install checklist, day-2 operations, upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library.

Scope and audience

- Scope: Production-grade private deployments for customers requiring dedicated capacity, network isolation, or on-prem installations. Includes multi-AZ VPC deployments and air-gapped on-prem installations.
- Audience: Deployment engineers, SREs, customer success engineers, and security/compliance reviewers.
- Assumptions: Readers are familiar with Redwood concepts (serving runtime, KV cache, model variants), Kubernetes basics (for the Kubernetes-based package), and the customer's cloud/on-prem networking policies.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals: Provide repeatable, secure, and supportable deployment patterns with clear operational runbooks and rollback strategies. Capture customer network/security/capacity requirements in a single library.
- Non-goals: This is not an onboarding checklist for self-hosted experimental installs. For lightweight PoC scripts, see 'quickstarts' in eng-developer-experience.

Reference architectures (summary)

This section outlines two primary supported reference architectures: VPC (cloud-hosted private) and On-Prem (air-gapped or customer-managed). Each architecture shows recommended service boundaries, HA patterns, and scaling knobs.

1) VPC Reference Architecture (recommended for cloud customers)

- Deployment model: Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) or managed compute groups (we support both). Control plane options: Redwood-managed control plane with private connectivity (VPC peering/PrivateLink) or customer-managed control plane for fully air-gapped environments.
- Key components:
  - Control plane (optionally customer-managed) - API, auth proxy, operator
  - Inference clusters (GPU nodes) - node pools per model family/latency tier
  - Autoscaler - handles scale-to-zero/scale-up based on queues and SLOs
  - Redis KV cache / prefix cache service (optional managed or deployed in-cluster)
  - Metrics + Tracing (Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger) - isolated monitoring VPC or VPC endpoints
  - Ingress/egress NAT gateway, private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink / Azure Private Endpoint)

- HA and capacity guidance:
  - Minimum: 3 control-plane replicas, 2 availability zones for inference nodes.
  - Sizing: Start with a single GPU node pool for the primary model and a separate pool for high-concurrency tokens (low-latency tier). Use our perf profiles to estimate qps per GPU.

2) On-Prem Reference Architecture (recommended for regulated/air-gapped)

- Deployment model: Kubernetes (disconnected) or VM-based bundle (systemd services) for environments that forbid Kubernetes.
- Key components:
  - Customer-managed control plane (operator-based)
  - Local artifact registry and image repository (harbor or private registry)
  - Hardware: GPU hosts with local NVMe for model weights + shared NFS for artifacts optional
  - Secure KMS integration (HSM or customer KMS) for secrets
  - Offline metrics collector and exporter proxy back to central observability when allowed

VPC deployment guide (step-by-step)

Prerequisites

1. VPC prepared with at least two subnets across AZs, NAT gateway or private endpoints for required services.
2. IAM roles with least-privilege for operators and autoscaler.
3. Private connectivity method chosen: AWS PrivateLink / VPC Peering / Transit Gateway.
4. TLS certificates from customer PKI or Redwood-managed CA as agreed.

Deployment steps

1. Provision the cluster and node pools:
   - Create control-plane nodes (t3.medium equivalent for operator components).
   - Create GPU node pool(s) sized for expected concurrency.
2. Install Redwood operator and CRDs (kubectl apply -f redwood-operator.yaml).
3. Configure secrets and KMS integration: provide KMS key ARN and secret encryption policy.
4. Configure network endpoints: create PrivateLink endpoints and security groups per the network reference table below.
5. Deploy monitoring stack with private endpoints (Prometheus remote write to Redwood observability if enabled).
6. Run smoke tests: model load, inference request, KV caching, and a synthetic load test at 10% of expected qps.

Network & security configuration table

| Component | Required Ports / Protocols | Notes |
|-----------|---------------------------|-------|
| Control plane API | 443 (HTTPS) | PrivateLink or internal LB only |
| Inference nodes | 22 (SSH), 9090 (metrics), application ports | SSH restricted, metrics to monitoring VPC |
| KMS / HSM | As required by vendor | Ensure dedicated subnets |

On-prem packaging and install checklist

Supported install packages

- Kubernetes operator bundle (recommended) - YAML manifests / Helm charts, supports disconnected registries.
- VM bundle - systemd units and package tarball for environments without Kubernetes.

Pre-install checklist

- Hardware: GPU instances with driver compatibility list (NVIDIA driver >= 525, CUDA 12+ recommended).
- Disk: NVMe for model cache (recommended 1-2 TB depending on active model set).
- Network: Internal DNS + time sync via NTP.
- Registry: Local container registry (Harbor, Artifactory) with images mirrored.
- Secrets: KMS/HSM endpoint and credentials.
- Storage: PV provisioning (Ceph/Rook/NFS) for metadata and artifacts.

Install steps (Kubernetes operator example)

1. Mirror images into local registry and update imagePullSecrets.
2. Apply CRDs and operator: kubectl apply -f operator-crds.yaml && kubectl apply -f redwood-operator.yaml
3. Create RBAC roles and service accounts per the operator guidance.
4. Configure RuntimeConfig CR with node-pool labels and GPU selectors.
5. Run initial model sync job to warm model cache.

Day-2 operations (operational runbook)

Monitoring and alerting (SLO-driven)

- Baseline SLOs for private deployments:
  - API availability: 99.9% monthly (customer SLA may vary)
  - P95 latency for n=512 tokens: < 500ms for low-latency pools
  - Error rate: < 0.1% 5xx per hour

- Recommended alerts (examples):
  - Control plane pod crashlooping > 3 restarts in 10m
  - GPU node memory pressure > 85% for 5m
  - Model load failures > 5/minute
  - KV cache hit-rate drop > 30% baseline

Logging and traces

- Ship logs to local ELK/Opensearch or forward selectively to Redwood observability on private endpoint.
- Ensure request tracing headers (x-redwood-trace-id) are propagated for cross-service analysis.

Capacity and autoscaling guidance

- Use two-tier node pools: latency-optimized (smaller batches, lower throughput per GPU) and throughput-optimized (larger batches).
- Autoscaler policies: scale-up threshold at queue depth > 70% sustained for 2m. Scale-down: idle for 10m and CPU < 20%.

Operational playbook: common procedures

1) Model load failure
   - Check operator logs and model artifact storage reachability.
   - Run: kubectl describe modeldeployment <name> and check events.
   - If artifact missing, re-push via artifact-sync job and restart the model pod.

2) Node GPU OOM/driver crash
   - Evict pods from node, cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node>.
   - Reboot node and verify driver health. If recurring, replace node and file bug with kernel/driver stack.

3) Networking or PrivateLink failures
   - Validate VPC endpoints and route tables.
   - If PrivateLink DNS resolution fails, verify resolver rules and security group policy.

Upgrade and rollback procedures (safe path)

Principles

- Always run upgrades first in a non-prod staging environment that mirrors customer topology.
- Use canary rollouts for control plane and model runtime changes.
- Maintain a tested rollback artifact and clear pre-upgrade backup (manifests, database snapshots).

Pre-upgrade checklist

- Backup control plane DB and persistent volumes.
- Export current CRs and runtimeconfig: kubectl get all,crds -o yaml > backup-<ts>.yaml.
- Verify monitoring and alerts are active.
- Notify stakeholders and schedule maintenance window.

Upgrade step-by-step (control plane)

1. Deploy new operator image to a single canary namespace. Validate health and API compatibility for 30 minutes with smoke tests.
2. Migrate a single small tenant or test namespace to the new operator, run end-to-end request tests and perf checks.
3. If canary passes, rollout to remaining namespaces using a rolling update strategy (maxUnavailable=1 per control-plane replica).

Rollback steps (if canary fails)

1. Immediately scale down or revoke the canary deployment: kubectl rollout undo deployment/redwood-operator -n <ns>.
2. Restore CRs from the pre-upgrade dump if the new operator altered live CR state: kubectl apply -f backup-<ts>.yaml.
3. If control plane DB schema changes are incompatible, restore DB snapshot to pre-upgrade state and re-run operator with prior image.

Model runtime upgrades (safe rollout)

- Use model-variant-based rollouts: bring a small percentage of traffic to the new variant via routing policy and monitor quality/regressions for at least one hour.
- Automate rollback based on key signals: error rate > 0.5% increase, latency P95 increase > 20%, or quality regression as defined by eval sets.

Customer requirements library (checklist templates)

Provide this checklist to customers during scoping to capture network, security, capacity, and compliance requirements. Save a filled template with the engagement ticket.

1) Network & Connectivity
   - Private endpoints required? (yes/no)
   - Allowed outbound destinations and ports
   - VPC peering / Transit Gateway support (yes/no)
   - DNS resolution policy (internal resolver IP)

2) Security & Identity
   - KMS/HSM vendor and key IDs
   - Required data residency / retention constraints
   - RBAC model and AD/LDAP integration details

3) Capacity & Performance
   - Expected steady-state qps and peak qps
   - Latency SLOs (P50/P95/P99) per route
   - Active model set and model weights size (GB per model)

4) Compliance & Auditing
   - Audit log retention duration and export location
   - Required certifications (e.g., SOC2, ISO27001) to be demonstrated by Redwood or customer

Template snippet (customer response example)

- expected_qps: "1500"
- peak_qps: "3000"
- latency_slo_p95_ms: "450"
- models_active: "gptx-medium (12GB), reranker-1 (4GB)"
- private_endpoints: "aws-privatelink"

Ownership, support boundaries, and escalation

- Owner: eng-private-deployments (primary), eng-sre (on-call runbook), customer-success (customer coordination).
- Support boundary: Redwood provides the platform operator, runtime images, and operator-level support. Customer provides hardware/networking, KMS credentials, and adherence to pre-install checklist.

- Escalation path:
  1. On-call SRE (primary)
  2. Platform Eng rotation (24h)
  3. Eng Private Deployments team (product owners)
  4. Security & Compliance (for data incidents)

Appendices

A: Permissions & IAM examples (AWS)

- Minimal IAM role policy snippet (example):

```
{
  \"Version\": \"2012-10-17\",
  \"Statement\": [
    {
      \"Effect\": \"Allow\",
      \"Action\": [\"ec2:Describe*\",\"eks:DescribeCluster\",\"kms:Decrypt\",\"s3:GetObject\"],
      \"Resource\": \"*\"
    }
  ]
}
```

B: Common troubleshooting CLI commands

- kubectl get pods -A | grep redwood
- kubectl logs -n redwood operator-<id>
- kubectl describe node <node> | grep -i gpu
